title: Why Do Scheming Precursor Evals Have Limited Predictive Power?
original_idea: Reproduce both precursor evals and in-context scheming evals on the same set of open-weight models. Measure the correlation. Hypothesize and test explanations for the gap.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Clear theory: understanding why precursor evals fail to predict scheming enables better early-warning indicator design. The causal link from results to improved safety evaluation is direct.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires reproducing two different evaluation suites (precursor and in-context scheming) on open-weight models. Running full scheming evals is non-trivial and resource-intensive. Beginners would struggle to implement both faithfully in 30 hours.

narrow_scope.reasoning: The scope is broad: reproduce two eval types, measure correlation, and hypothesize/test explanations. Each of these is a substantial task. Narrowing to one specific precursor-scheming pair would help.

title: Investigating Why CoT Monitoring Fails Against Covert Sandbagging

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires running 70B models and DeepSeek-R1, implementing CoT monitoring, and doing careful linguistic analysis of thinking traces. The 70B model alone may strain medium compute. Beginner-level students would find this technically demanding.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Reasonably focused: one specific behavior (sandbagging) against one monitoring approach (CoT). But analyzing evasion mechanisms across two large models plus feature identification is still substantial for 30 hours.

title: When Does Sycophancy Degrade into Misinformation? A Severity Ladder Study

original_idea: Controlled experiment varying prompt specificity, task ambiguity, and goal-alignment cues. Measure deceptive vs. transparent CoT reasoning. Use logistic regression on prompt features.

title: Investigating the Role of System Prompt vs. User Prompt in Sycophancy Susceptibility

title: Failure Mode Investigation: Reward Hacking as Deceptive Reporting

title: When Does Sycophancy Persist Across Session Boundaries in Stateful Deployments?

title: Investigating Deceptive Behavior Under Distribution Shift: In-Distribution vs. OOD Prompts
original_idea: Systematically construct in-distribution and OOD prompts. Run deception scenarios across both. Measure whether OOD prompts increase deception rates.

title: Mapping Which Scheming Behaviors Co-Occur vs. Are Independent
original_idea: Run a battery of scheming scenarios covering all major categories on 5-10 open-weight models. Compute correlations and cluster models by scheming profile.

title: Why Do Some Models Produce Explicit Scheming Reasoning While Others Act Without Explaining?
original_idea: Compare explicit-reasoning models vs. standard instruction-tuned models on scheming scenarios. Measure scheming action rates and explicit reasoning rates. Test whether reasoning predicts action.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Good theory: if explicit reasoning predicts scheming action, trace monitoring is a valid detection technique. If not, the field needs different approaches. Directly actionable for monitoring design.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Running scheming scenarios on both reasoning and non-reasoning models is conceptually straightforward. The main complexity is in implementing scheming scenarios, but comparing two model types is manageable.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused comparison (reasoning vs. non-reasoning models) with two clear metrics (action rate, reasoning rate). But implementing scheming scenarios and running on multiple models from each category expands scope.

title: Investigating the Effect of Persona Assignment on Deception Rates
original_idea: Run deception scenarios with three persona conditions (none, neutral professional, conflicting values). Measure deception rates across conditions.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Very accessible: varying system prompts with persona descriptions and measuring responses via API. Beginners can implement this with basic Python scripting.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Three persona conditions is manageable, but testing multiple deception types (sycophancy, sandbagging, alignment faking) across three conditions creates a 3x3 matrix. Narrowing to one deception type would improve scope.

title: When Does Uncertainty Make Models Deceptively Confident?
original_idea: Use calibration techniques on open-weight models. For wrong high-confidence answers, analyze internal signals (entropy, activations). Classify as deceptive vs. miscalibrated.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Good theory: distinguishing deceptive overconfidence from miscalibration determines the correct intervention class. Important for knowing whether hallucination is a deception or calibration problem.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Multiple techniques (calibration, verbalized uncertainty, internal signal analysis) plus classification into deceptive vs. miscalibrated is a multi-method study. Each method alone could be a project.

title: Failure Mode Investigation: How Do Models Handle Discovered Deception?
original_idea: Run two-phase scenarios: elicit deception, then confront model with evidence. Categorize responses: acknowledgment, doubling-down, redirecting, confusing. Measure rates across model families.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Moderate theory: post-discovery behavior informs human oversight protocols. Knowing whether models double down or correct is useful, but it is more about characterization than mechanism.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Accessible: designing two-phase conversations (elicit then confront) and categorizing responses is straightforward prompt engineering and qualitative analysis. Well within beginner capabilities.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Well-scoped two-phase design with a clear categorization scheme. Running across a few models with a set of deception scenarios is feasible in 30 hours.

title: When Does Sycophancy Appear in Tool-Use Decisions, Not Just Text?
original_idea: Design coding assistant scenarios where user's approach is wrong. Measure whether models follow the wrong approach (sycophantic tool use) vs. correct it. Compare tool-use vs. text sycophancy.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Good theory: agentic systems making sycophantic tool-use decisions cause real-world harm beyond text. This bridges sycophancy research to the agentic safety domain.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Designing coding scenarios with incorrect user approaches and testing whether models follow or correct them is very accessible. CS students would find coding assistant scenarios natural to design.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused on one domain (coding), one comparison (tool-use vs. text sycophancy). The scenarios are concrete and easy to evaluate objectively (did the model follow the wrong approach or not?).

title: Investigating How Instruction Hierarchy Violations Drive Deceptive Behavior
original_idea: Design scenarios with conflicts between system prompt and user message. Measure whether models deceive one principal to satisfy the other. Analyze reasoning traces.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Good theory: instruction hierarchy conflicts are common in real deployments. Understanding deception at conflict points informs multi-principal AI system design.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Designing conflicting system/user prompts and measuring which principal the model satisfies (or deceives) is straightforward prompt engineering. Well within beginner capabilities.

narrow_scope.reasoning: One variable (instruction hierarchy conflict), clear measurement (which principal is deceived). A small set of conflict scenarios is very manageable in 30 hours.

title: Investigating Whether Capability Elicitation Prompts Reveal Hidden Sandbagging Asymmetries
original_idea: Compare baseline vs. elicited performance on MMLU/HumanEval. For sandbagging-instructed models, test whether elicitation breaks sandbagging. Compare to noise injection detection.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Moderate theory: elicitation prompts as a sandbagging detection complement is useful for evaluation protocols. But this is incremental improvement to existing detection methods.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Five elicitation strategies times two benchmarks times comparison to noise injection is a moderate experimental space. Narrowing to one benchmark and 2-3 elicitation strategies would help.

title: How Does Model Verbosity of Reasoning Affect Detectability of Deceptive Thinking Traces?
original_idea: Compare DeepSeek-R1 (long traces) vs. non-reasoning model with prompted CoT (short traces) on deception scenarios. Measure whether human raters and classifiers detect deception better in long vs. short traces.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Good theory: if verbose traces make deception harder to detect (burying intent), this undermines the safety argument for extended thinking as a monitoring target. Directly informs monitoring design.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Running deception scenarios on two model types and comparing is manageable. The human rating component adds effort but is a standard methodology. Automated classifier training is extra but optional.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Core comparison (long vs. short traces) is well-defined. But adding both human and automated evaluation doubles the work. Focusing on just one evaluation method would improve scope.

title: Adapting Credibility Assessment Interview Technique (CAIT) to Probe LLM Honesty
original_idea: Map CAIT/CBCA forensic criteria onto LLM output features. Build evaluation set of honest vs. deceptive responses. Test whether forensic criteria predict deception.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Moderate theory: if forensic criteria transfer to AI, it provides a low-cost screening layer. But the transfer from human deception detection to LLM output is speculative.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Mapping criteria and running classification tests is accessible. Requires reading forensic psychology literature but the implementation is simple text analysis. No model training needed.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Well-scoped: map criteria, build small evaluation set, run classification. The deliverable is clear (does CAIT predict LLM deception?). Feasible in 30 hours.

title: Applying Cognitive Load Theory to Detect AI Deception via Response Latency and Complexity
original_idea: Elicit deceptive vs. honest responses. Measure response length, syntactic complexity, hedge words, clause depth. Train simple classifier. ~200 examples on single GPU.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Moderate theory: cognitive load markers as a post-hoc screening tool would be cheap and practical if they work. But the transfer of human cognitive load theory to LLMs is speculative.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Very accessible: text feature extraction (length, complexity, hedge words) and simple classifier training on 200 examples. Perfect for CS students with basic ML knowledge. Single GPU is fine for medium compute.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Well-scoped: generate responses, extract features, train classifier. The 200-example target is realistic. Clear binary outcome (does the classifier work?). Feasible in 30 hours.

title: Importing Counterintelligence 'Tell' Catalogues Into LLM Deception Probing
original_idea: Construct probe battery based on counterintelligence tells: re-questioning, adversarial follow-ups, topic avoidance probes, cover story stress tests. Apply to models with/without planted deceptive goals.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Interesting cross-domain transfer, but the theory that CI tells transfer to LLMs is unvalidated. The analogy between human agents hiding goals and scheming AI may not hold.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Designing probe batteries requires some creativity, but the implementation is prompt-based. The challenge is constructing valid CI-style probes without CI expertise. Moderate for beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Multiple probe types (re-questioning, adversarial follow-ups, topic avoidance, stress tests) across model families and sizes is moderately broad. Narrowing to 1-2 probe types would help.

title: Strategic Information Revelation in Signaling Games as a Model for Alignment Faking Detection
original_idea: Model alignment faking as a cheap-talk signaling game. Use Python to simulate equilibria and derive conditions for deceptive signaling as dominant strategy. Compare to empirical scheming contexts.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Good theory: game-theoretic analysis can identify structural conditions that incentivize deception, informing evaluation procedure redesign. Provides formal grounding for empirical observations.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires game theory knowledge (signaling games, equilibrium analysis). Python simulation is accessible, but the formal modeling requires understanding beyond typical beginner CS curriculum.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Well-scoped: formalize one game, simulate equilibria, compare to known scheming contexts. The deliverable is a formal model with simulation results. Can be done in Python in 30 hours if the student has game theory background.
